A.explanation: A $50 \text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ sweep is far too slow, as one $20 \text{ }\mu\text{s}$ cycle would occupy only a tiny fraction of a cm.

B.explanation: A $1 \text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ sweep is still about 50 times too slow, so many thousands of cycles would overlap on the screen.

C.explanation: With $10 \text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$ one $20 \text{ }\mu\text{s}$ period occupies $2 \text{ cm}$, giving a clear display of a few cycles.

D.explanation: A $0.5 \text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$ sweep is too fast, as one $20 \text{ }\mu\text{s}$ period would need $40 \text{ cm}$ and would not fit on the screen.

hints: Start from the given $50 \text{ kHz}$ signal frequency and work out the time for one complete cycle using $T = 1/f$.
Convert $50 \text{ kHz}$ to $50000 \text{ Hz}$ and check that the period is in microseconds, not milliseconds.
Remember the time-base in $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is the time per horizontal cm, so you want one $20 \text{ }\mu\text{s}$ cycle to span about $2 \text{ cm}$ on a typical screen.
walkthrough: Identify the given information: signal frequency $f = 50 \text{ kHz} = 50000 \text{ Hz}$.
Use the period-frequency relation $T = 1/f$ to find the time of one cycle.
Substitute values with units: $T = 1/50000 \text{ s} = 0.00002 \text{ s} = 20 \text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
Recall that the time-base setting is the time represented by $1 \text{ cm}$ horizontally, so the width of one cycle is $T$ divided by the time-base.

For $10 \text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$, width $= 20 \text{ }\mu\text{s} / 10 \text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1} = 2 \text{ cm}$, so about 4 to 5 cycles fit across a $10 \text{ cm}$ screen, which is ideal for investigation.
The ms settings would compress thousands of cycles together and the $0.5 \text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$ setting would make one cycle far wider than the screen. This is option C.
